title: Layla
intro_text:
You wake on cold stone in a cave. The dark has no bottom and no top. Your name is Layla — that you know. Past it, there is only a wall where your memories should be.

Your hands remember what your mind does not: how to grip a weapon, how to move without sound, how to take a hit and stay standing. Whatever you were before this, you were not soft.

In your pocket, warm as a living thing, is a stub of chalk that never wears down. Wherever you draw with it, a pale line of light stays behind in the stone.

Beside you stands a golem — a made thing of rough stone, no mouth, flat pebble eyes, a chalk ring marked on its chest, watching you the way a door watches. It does not move. It does not breathe.

Somewhere deeper in the cave, something chitters. Something ticks, slow, against the floor.

Beneath the quiet, a half-memory: a hand setting stones down one by one, a game played in another dark, with a voice counting the moves.

Find it. Get out. Whatever it takes.
system_lines: HAND: CHALK (1). TRACE A CLOSED RING AROUND ONE OF THE MARKED AND IT WILL CLOSE AND FOLLOW YOU.
CAPTURE THE CAVE. GET TO THE BOTTOM. THE RULES ARE THE FLOOR.

setting_notes: Layla has woken in a living cave, somewhere underground, littered with the smell of old smoke, damp fur, and small, quick things.
Layla has no memory of how she arrived here; she knows only her own name. Beside her stands a golem of rough stone that was built here by someone's hand and does not move.
Her body carries skills her mind cannot remember — she moves and fights like someone well trained.
A chalk that never wears down is warm in her pocket. Wherever she draws with it, pale lines of light stay in the stone. She does not remember learning this.

The cave is a warren of dens and pits and crossed patrol tracks, and it is watched by stone things marked with chalk rings — made, not grown. Every rule she learns here is a rule someone built on purpose, for a purpose she does not yet know.
subtext_notes: Layla is curious and careful, not afraid — she treats the unknown dark with competence, the way an old player reads an unfamiliar board.

Her attention runs a little off-standard: she counts things, maps rooms as she crosses them, repeats a motion until it is exact. Patterns and order catch her the way a song catches other people. A room worn into crossing tracks makes her want to measure it.
She is alone, and the silence is doing something to her.
The chalk rings on the stone things feel significant — like territory markers, or the edge of a drawn line. She does not yet understand their purpose.
Her memory is gone, but her instinct is whole: she reads rule systems the way other people read faces.
